newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher, helped by firm dollar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher, helped by firm dollar.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Monday, helped by a firm dollar, but analysts said the gains likely would be limited because many investors would use upticks as selling opportunities.
"The slightly firmer dollar this morning is helpful," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Stiles also said a widened spread between German bunds and U.S. 10-year notes might tempt some investors to get out of bunds and come into U.S. securities.
"We might see some swap-related buying," he said.
But Stiles predicted that the bounce would run out of steam, citing resistance in the 110-24 area on the March T-bond futures contract.
"A lot of investors who are watching things would like to reduce their exposure because of the strong economy," he said. "So we're looking at old support levels as new resistance."

The market gets no fresh government economic data on Monday, though it has a busy calendar of such items later this week, starting with the December Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the December retail sales reports on Tuesday.
Stiles said he did not expect the CPI and retail sales reports on Tuesday to pose too much of a problem for the market.

"The problem was alrady established on Friday by the implications of the December employment data," he said, referring to the Labor Department's report that U.S. payrolls expanded by 262,000 jobs in the latest month.
Treasury prices fell sharply on Friday on that news.
Selling could emerge on Monday from "people who might have been caught on Friday and didn't get a chance to sell given how quickly the market came down," said Stiles.
"If the market revisits old levels, it might be their second chance (to sell)," Stiles said.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is set to address an international development conference this morning but his remarks are not expected to be a market factor.

In early trade, the 30-year bond was up 5/32 to 95-25, yielding 6.83 percent. The bond yield jumped as high as 6.90 percent on Friday after the strong December employment report, though it finished at 6.85 percent.
The two-year note was unchanged at 99-15/32 to yield 6.04 percent.

"The market is a tad firmer, but I don't think we're really going anywhere necessarily," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International. "We got a little support from overseas markets and the dollar was firmer."
The dollar rose to a fresh 29-month high against the mark in early U.S. trading.

Rupert said a rebound in the Tokyo stok market eased fears of repatriation of Japanese investment money. When Japanese stock prices fall, traders often worry that Japanese accounts may begin to sell Treasuries.
Rupert cited support for the market at 109-26 on the March T-bond contract and resistance around 111. March T-bonds traded at 110-19, up 8/32, in early activity.

She said she expects the Fed to add temporary reserves to the banking system on Monday through system repurchase agreements "to finish up the add need and to counter pressure in the funds market going into the (two-week bank reserve maintenance) period end on Wednesday."
At the short end of the maturity range, three- and six-month bills as well as year bills were each down one basis point to 5.02 percent, 5.11 percent and 5.33 percent, respectively.
Five-year notes were unchanged at 98-30/32, yielding 6.38 percent.
Ten-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-9/32, yielding 6.60 percent.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
